cells.tense: You are at this threshold with both hands open, naming what you tend as it comes, here and not later
cells.ask: Pick the one thing you are already tending and tell one other person plainly what you put into it, before the day closes.
cells.core: What tends well here looks like a kitchen where the pot gets stirred before anyone asks, where the small arrival is met and nobody has to be reminded twice. You can carry two demands at the same time and let neither one lose — the work, the person, the thing nobody else picked up. That kind of care does not run a person down, and the ones near it can feel the difference.\n\nWhat hasn't happened yet is anyone saying so out loud, including you. Something finished here deserves to be seen, and seeing it is not vanity. It sets the next thing free. Pick the one you mean, say it plainly, and let someone hear what you put in.

cells.tense: You are leaning over a future that has not arrived to ask something of it, and the lean is what is costing you now
cells.ask: Leave one thing you are responsible for to run three days without your adjustments, and write down only what actually changed.
cells.core: Handled well, this looks like a workshop bench where the tools are already sharpened and the next job set out before the last one finishes, steady and unhurried. It is the same steadiness that is now running a season ahead of you, doing next month's work in this one.\n\nThe tending itself is sound and the forcing has outrun the thing being tended. What belongs to next month is being paid for today, and nothing arrives faster for the payment. Let one thing stay unmanaged for three days, keep a plain note of what actually changed, and let the note carry the whole point.

cells.tense: The door you are still standing at is behind you, so what arrives meets someone who has stepped back from it
cells.ask: Name one thing in your care that still has a pulse, water it once today, and write one line about what you noticed.
cells.core: A threshold kept well has someone at it who feeds what arrives, lets it grow at its own pace, and keeps the hands loose — present, unhurried, not bracing for the next thing. That version wears a person down less, and it does not need a mood to get started.\n\nWhat arrives now meets a version of you that has stepped back while still watching. Something still alive in your keeping hasn't been fed, and feeding it doesn't need a decision sitting in front of it — one small act of care counts as the whole thing. Pick the one with a pulse, water it once today, and let the line you write stay small and plain.

cells.tense: You are already steering what enters this room and the pen is in your hand, though you haven't said so to yourself
cells.ask: Later today, say out loud to one person: this thing is mine to see to. Leave the next sentence theirs.
cells.core: A threshold kept well has someone who picks up the small arrivals, lets them grow at their own pace, doesn't stage it, and doesn't keep a list. Something close to that is already running here, filed under just how things go.\n\nMore stays alive in your care than you would put on paper, and a fair amount of it got called what has to happen anyway. Setting your name on one of them out loud, once, shows you where the edge of it sits — what's yours and where somebody else begins. It lightens tomorrow, and it asks no one else to carry anything.
